reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Characterised by a clinical triad of early joint contractures, slowly progressive muscle weakness, and cardiac involvement
The X-linked form is caused by EMD variants (emerin) and the autosomal dominant form by LMNA variants (lamin A/C), with less common recessive and other causes
Contractures typically develop early at the elbows, Achilles tendons, and posterior neck, often preceding significant weakness
Weakness follows a humeroperoneal distribution, affecting the upper arms and lower legs before spreading more widely
Cardiac disease features conduction block, atrial arrhythmia with a risk of atrial standstill and thromboembolism, and cardiomyopathy, and can cause sudden death
Cardiac involvement may occur even with mild skeletal weakness, so all patients need regular cardiac surveillance and consideration of a pacemaker or defibrillator
Female carriers of the X-linked form and relatives with LMNA variants can develop life-threatening cardiac disease and require screening
Diagnosis combines the clinical triad with molecular genetic testing and, where needed, muscle biopsy with emerin or lamin immunostaining
reference.pathophysiology: Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy is caused by defects in proteins of the nuclear envelope: emerin, encoded by EMD, and lamin A/C, encoded by LMNA. These proteins provide structural support to the inner nuclear membrane and participate in nuclear organisation, mechanotransduction, and gene regulation. Loss or dysfunction leaves nuclei mechanically fragile, particularly in tissues subjected to repetitive strain such as skeletal and cardiac muscle. The resulting nuclear injury and disturbed gene expression produce progressive muscle weakness, early contractures, and the conduction-system disease and cardiomyopathy that make cardiac complications the most dangerous feature of the disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies, including LMNA-related forms
Bethlem myopathy and other collagen VI-related contracture disorders
Other causes of inherited cardiomyopathy with conduction disease
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of EMD and LMNA, with a wider panel if needed
Electrocardiography and prolonged rhythm monitoring for conduction disease and arrhythmia
Echocardiography or cardiac MRI for cardiomyopathy
Serum creatine kinase, which is normal or mildly to moderately elevated
Muscle biopsy with emerin or lamin A/C immunostaining in selected cases
Cardiac screening of at-risk relatives and X-linked carriers
redFlags: Syncope, palpitations, or high-grade conduction block indicating risk of sudden death
Atrial arrhythmia or atrial standstill with thromboembolic risk
Signs of progressive cardiomyopathy or heart failure
New cardiac symptoms in a known carrier or affected relative
Severe contractures compromising function or respiratory mechanics
reference.prognosis: Skeletal muscle weakness usually progresses slowly, but prognosis is dominated by cardiac disease, which can cause sudden death even in patients with mild weakness. Timely cardiac device therapy, anticoagulation for arrhythmia, and heart-failure management substantially improve survival.
pitfalls: Concentrating on muscle weakness while overlooking the potentially fatal cardiac disease
Assuming female carriers of the X-linked form are free of cardiac risk
Delaying pacemaker or defibrillator consideration despite documented conduction disease
Missing early contractures as a clue to the diagnosis
Neglecting cardiac screening of relatives with LMNA variants
